content: Endometriosis is a condition characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue, including both stromal and glandular components, outside the normal uterine cavity. Conventional treatments, both medical and surgical, aim to either remove or reduce these ectopic endometrial deposits. It has been observed that states of hyperandrogenism, which involve an excess of male hormones, can lead to atrophy of the endometrium. This observation has formed the basis for the use of androgens in the treatment of endometriosis. Danazol is one such androgen-based treatment. The therapeutic efficacy of danazol lies in its ability to create a hormonal environment characterized by high androgen levels and low estrogen levels, effectively mimicking a state of pseudo-menopause. This hormonal shift induces atrophy of the endometriotic implants, leading to a reduction in associated pain and other symptoms. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of danazol, compared to either placebo or no treatment, in alleviating the symptoms and clinical signs of endometriosis, excluding infertility, in women of reproductive age. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Specialised Register of trials (as of April 2007), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, Issue 2, 2007), and MEDLINE (from 1966 to April 2007). Additionally, reference lists of included trials were reviewed, and pharmaceutical companies were contacted to obtain information on unpublished trials. The inclusion criteria for this analysis were limited to randomized controlled trials that compared danazol, either as a standalone treatment or as an adjunct to surgery, with placebo or no therapy. Trials that exclusively reported infertility outcomes were excluded from the review. Ultimately, five trials met the inclusion criteria. Data extraction from these trials was performed independently by two authors. All five trials compared danazol to placebo. Three of these trials evaluated danazol as a sole therapy, while the remaining three assessed its use as an adjunct to surgical intervention. Although the primary outcome of interest was pain relief, additional data on laparoscopic scores and hormonal parameters were also collected. The results demonstrated that treatment with danazol, whether used alone or in conjunction with surgery, was effective in alleviating painful symptoms associated with endometriosis when compared to placebo. Furthermore, laparoscopic scores, which assess the extent of endometriotic lesions, showed improvement with danazol treatment, both as a standalone therapy and as an adjunct to surgery, when compared to placebo or no treatment. However, the use of danazol was associated with a higher incidence of side effects, particularly those of an androgenic nature, in comparison to placebo. In conclusion, danazol is an effective treatment for the symptoms and signs of endometriosis. Nevertheless, its clinical utility is limited by the occurrence of androgenic side effects, which may impact patient tolerance and adherence to therapy.
